title: Spotify ramps up policy enforcement on family plans
gist: Spotify is enforcing its same-address rule for Family and Duo plans by requiring members to scan a QR code in person on the plan manager's device within seven days or drop to the free tier and be barred from such plans for 12 months. The move follows an October 15 Goldman Sachs report that says many family-plan users are not household members and sees monetization upside in tighter verification, much like Netflix's 2023 password-sharing crackdown, which preceded 9.3 million added subscriptions and a 54 percent jump in operating income.

insights.claim: Spotify now requires Family and Duo plan members to scan a QR code in person on the plan manager's device; those who do not within seven days are downgraded to the free tier and barred from joining any Duo or Family plan for 12 months.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Tighter enforcement should push some sharers into paid individual plans and lift revenue per user.
insights.locator: As reported by Music Business Worldwide

insights.claim: The enforcement rests on Spotify's existing rule that family plan members live at the same address, and Spotify's support documentation confirmed it after Reddit users reported getting the prompt.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: This enforces an existing policy rather than adding a new one, so it needs no new terms.

insights.claim: Indge warns the policy could hit genuine families split by distance, such as a child at college or a spouse who travels for work, not just friends sharing to save money.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Some churn and backlash risk among legitimate subscribers.

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs analysts, in their October 15 Music in the Air: 10 Years On report, estimate a meaningful share of family plan users are friends rather than household members, and see monetization upside from tightening household verification because enforcement has been minimal.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Sell-side framing of household verification as a revenue lever for music streaming services.
insights.quote: We see additional monetization upside from tightening household verification on multi-user plans.
insights.locator: Goldman Sachs analysts, in their October 15

insights.claim: Goldman argues family plans' per-user monetization materially lags individual pricing and offers more value than the individual tier, giving music streaming services room to raise prices or tighten eligibility without meaningfully hurting demand.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Suggests streaming services have pricing power and family-plan ARPU could rise.
insights.quote: the per-user monetization of these plans materially lags individual plan pricing

insights.claim: Streaming services tend to tolerate account sharing while growing and crack down once users are hooked: Netflix tweeted that love is sharing a password in March 2017, then launched enforcement in May 2023.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: A repeatable playbook for monetizing mature subscription platforms.

insights.claim: Netflix raised prices up to 17 percent later in 2023, and by April 2024 its crackdown had paid off with 9.3 million added subscriptions and a 54 percent rise in operating income.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: A quantified precedent for the upside Spotify could see from enforcement.

insights.claim: Max (now HBO again) and Disney+/Hulu followed Netflix with their own account-sharing enforcement.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Sharing crackdowns are now standard across subscription media.
insights.locator: Netflix isn’t alone in the practice
